excluded.reason: Most of the recording is narrated slides, labeled anatomy, and annotated sonograms. Candidate current/history answers are exposed by slide labels or ASR; delayed transitions are scripted slide cuts or sonographic changes that cannot be timed and verified reliably from the reviewed frames. Four natural visual-dependent QA with two genuinely delayed answers could not be supported without padding.

The candidate clinical anatomy, needle adjustment, and injection-result answers are narrated almost directly; the relevant sonograms are partly labeled or visually too subtle to establish unique first-sufficient delayed answers. The rest of the recording consists mainly of illustrated slides and text cards. A four-type, visual-dependent, balanced QA set would be forced.

The educational montage labels the anatomy and approach, and ASR explicitly narrates nerve position, needle route, fascial-plane spread, and nerve visibility. The unannotated sonograms reviewed at 194.5, 214.5, 244.5, and 264.5 seconds do not support reliable visually distinct onset times for two delayed clinical questions. Only slide transitions would provide easy delayed triggers, which are low-value template shortcuts.

Throughout the ultrasound tutorial, the same on-screen captions describe the probe movement and identify the cecum, vessels, target-shaped appendix, and longitudinal blind end. The ASR gives the same sequence. Proposed QA can be answered from visible text/narration rather than interpreting the sonogram, including prospective delayed questions.

The video is a patient-information interview with noncontiguous illustrative clinic cutaways, not a continuous visual record of one biopsy. The ASR fully describes preparation, sampling, clip placement, dressing, and aftercare. Visual cutaway changes cannot safely ground procedural progression or notification timing; questions about clinic props would be trivial.

The actual scanning segment is dominated by a nearly fixed split-screen sonogram/probe view. The ASR states nerve position, needle approach, and local-anesthetic spread; in the reviewed original-resolution one-second grid, late fluid change is too subtle to assign a reliable first-sufficient answer time. Two possible delayed questions would both concern the same brief Doppler/position adjustment and lack type diversity.

The recording is a narrated teaching montage with arrows, labels, on-screen instructions and a probe-position diagram. The normal appendix, ileocecal valve, psoas, CT comparison, appendicitis and fat wrap are announced or labeled at the relevant time. This creates answer leakage for the four requested QA categories, and the noncontiguous inserted examples make delayed clinical trigger times ambiguous.

The video is an explicit narrated slide/tutorial. Its probe orientation, vein/artery labels, compression behavior, Doppler behavior, medial/lateral relationships and long-axis tube appearance are all simultaneously spelled out in ASR and on-screen text/arrows. Without relying on trivia about props, a visual-primary immediate/delayed 1:1 set cannot be formed.

The recording is a schematic probe/needle manipulation lesson rather than an observed clinical scan. The ASR explicitly explains every named movement and its resulting image, while large on-screen labels identify sliding, compression, rocking, tilting, needle visibility and alignment. Delayed question triggers would mostly be animation/cut transitions predictable from narration or text.

This lecture compares display conventions through a rotating anatomical model and paired ultrasound clips. The key mirror-image, screen-marker, and probe-orientation facts are explicitly narrated and later printed on the frames; remaining visual queries would be about incidental illustration geometry or lecture editing, not a meaningful ultrasound observation.

The video is a hand-held needle/probe demonstration over a striped paper schematic, without an actual ultrasound scan or patient target. Its clinically meaningful in-plane/out-of-plane and needle-following facts are fully narrated in ASR. Candidate questions about which hand holds which object or arbitrary paper position would make visual dependence trivial rather than meaningful; no defensible 4-type, 1:1 AV set was retained.

The FAST lecture consists of a presenter plus static labeled slides and example still sonograms. The clinically useful findings, including free-fluid locations, are directly annotated with arrows/text and narrated. No visually evolving patient examination supports a causal delayed question.

The internal-jugular lecture largely shows static or repeated annotated sonograms and probe-position graphics. Vein/artery locations, Valsalva enlargement, and long-axis flow direction are explicitly written or spoken; no distinct visual-first delayed clinical transition remains after removing edit-cut and label-reading questions.

The entire liver protocol is a sequence of labeled static ultrasound stills paired with probe-position diagrams. Each organ/vessel and probe orientation is named in the image and narrated. Slide transitions would create artificial WAIT/ANSWER timing.

Probe-orientation lecture uses diagrams and screen labels while the narration explicitly gives the directional mapping and sequence. Under the visual-first rule, the candidate immediate answers are supplied by ASR and prospective events reduce to slide/annotation transitions; four useful visual-dependent QA cannot be justified.

Pleural-effusion lesson is dominated by text-labeled ultrasound slides. The captions and narration identify the anatomical structures and effusion grades; proposed temporal/event answers would be predictable from slide labels or edit order rather than independent sonographic observation.

Spinal-ultrasound lecture is dominated by labeled anatomy animations, annotated still sonograms, and text slides. Candidate answers about landmarks and approach are carried by labels/narration; delayed questions reduce to slide transitions rather than a newly observed clinical condition.

The thyroid FNA lesson contains a short real-neck anesthesia sequence and a phantom demonstration, but the core anatomy, biopsy steps and expected change in skin appearance are explicitly narrated or written on slides. The remaining purely visual details are incidental setup details; four meaningful visual-primary questions with two genuinely unresolved delayed triggers cannot be supported.

The same sequence is narrated; four useful visual-dependent QA, including two delayed changes, would largely test reading the overlay or predicting the edited tutorial order.

The central-line Part 2 video is largely explanatory slides, annotated ultrasound clips, and verbatim narration of the needle/wire appearances. Candidate QA can be answered from slide text or ASR, while prospective events are mostly pre-edited clip changes rather than a meaningful unresolved visual condition.

review_limitations: Same-assistant question-led sampled self-review of original-resolution frames; not continuous full-video viewing.
ASR was read but original audio was not directly listened to during QA authorship.
No clinical expert review, independent blind review, or model ablation has been performed.
Only query and answer checkpoints are labelled for delayed tasks; intervening seconds are not exhaustively labelled.
acceptance_note: The original video-type and per-stage value labels remain authoritative selection context. The 29 original exclusions used an overly strict per-video QA quota and ad hoc near-duplicate exclusion; they require question-level re-review before final rejection. Current counts describe the existing draft only.
